name: Ken Olsen
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: computerhistory.org/profile/ken-olsen/ names him a 1996 CHM Fellow, citation 'For his introduction of the minicomputer as cofounder Digital Equipment Corporation'. SERIAL FOUNDER CHECK: no earlier venture found -- en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Olsen and the IEEE ETHW biography both place him on MIT staff continuously from 1950 until he and Harlan Anderson left to found DEC in 1957; DEC is his first company. BOUNDED rev10 1959-1960, both ends sourced. LOWER end: DEC's first-year module sales were $94,000 in 1958 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Equipment_Corporation), about 10% of the 1958 nominal bar of $897,674, so the crossing is not before 1959. UPPER end: Britannica Money's DEC entry states DEC in 1960 was 'a local computer company with 117 employees and $1.3 million in revenue'; $1,300,000 is 141% of the 1960 nominal bar of $919,417 (rev10 = $10M constant 2026), a 41% margin. No FY1959 or FY1961 figure exists after two source attempts (targeted searches plus DEC's own 1978 corporate history 'Nineteen Fifty-Seven to the Present', s3data.computerhistory.org/pdp-1/dec.digital_1957_to_the_present_(1978).1957-1978.102630349.pdf, whose 1957-1963 financial summary prints only FY1962 $6,535,502 and FY1963 $9,906,968), hence the bound rather than a pinned year. The IPO fallback is barred anyway: the 1966 listing is six years after a documented above-bar year. NOTE the widely reprinted FundingUniverse/Encyclopedia.com line calling $1.2M '1963 revenues' is net income, not revenue -- DEC's own FY1963 net sales were $9.9M -- and was not used. a2: MS in electrical engineering, MIT, 1952 (BS 1950). a3: 1950, staff of MIT's Digital Computer Laboratory / Lincoln Laboratory -- ETHW's IEEE biography says he was on that staff 'for seven years' before founding Digital in 1957. a6: 1965, first shipment of the PDP-8, the first commercially successful minicomputer and the thing he is known for (Britannica).

name: Steve Wozniak
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: computerhistory.org/profile/steve-wozniak/ names him a 1998 CHM Fellow, citation 'For co-founding Apple Computer and inventing the Apple I personal computer'. PINNED rev10 1978 from a PRIMARY source: Apple Computer, Inc.'s December 1980 IPO prospectus (scan at deramp.com/swtpc.com/Apple/Apple_IPO.pdf; identical copy at swtpc.com/files/mholley/apple/apple_ipo.pdf) prints the consolidated statement of income for every year of the company's life. Net sales from inception (January 3, 1977) to September 30, 1977 were $773,977 -- 41% of the 1977 nominal bar of $1,882,321, i.e. BELOW it. Net sales for fiscal 1978 (ended September 30, 1978) were $7,856,360, total revenues $7,883,486 -- 388% of the 1978 nominal bar of $2,025,203 (rev10 = $10M constant 2026), a 288% margin. Fiscal 1979 was $47,938,981. The crossing year is therefore fiscal 1978, pinned, not bounded, and the IPO fallback is not needed. SERIAL FOUNDER CHECK: two earlier Wozniak ventures exist and neither is close to the bar. (1) The blue boxes he designed and Jobs sold from late 1971, which Wikipedia calls 'their first business partnership' -- about 200 units at $150, roughly $30,000 gross, against a 1971 bar of $928,736-plus; that is a4. (2) The Apple I sold by the Jobs-Wozniak partnership from April 1976 before incorporation -- roughly 200 boards at $666.66, about $133,000, against the 1976 bar of $1,767,394. Neither crosses, so Apple Computer, Inc. is correctly the hit entity. a2 DROPOUT RULE: last credential actually COMPLETED before his career is the Homestead High School diploma, 1968 ('Wozniak graduated from Homestead High with honors in 1968', EBSCO Research Starters; handwiki mirror agrees). He was expelled from the University of Colorado Boulder after one year (1968-69, Britannica), attended De Anza College, transferred to UC Berkeley in 1971 and dropped out; he did later finish the Berkeley BS in EECS, but that was in 1986/1987 (Wikipedia says 1986, woz.org says 1987), eight years AFTER the hit, so it is a post-hit credential and is deliberately not used as the education-end anchor. a3: 'By 1973, Wozniak was working at Hewlett-Packard in Palo Alto' (EBSCO). An earlier computing job exists -- EBSCO says that after returning to California he 'got a job programming and running diagnostics on computers at Tenet, Inc.' -- but two source attempts (handwiki, Britannica, which says only 'during the early 1970s Wozniak worked at several small electronics firms') produced no year and no statement that it was full-time, so a3 is dated on the sourced HP year rather than inferring a Tenet year. a6: December 1980 IPO.

name: Amancio Ortega
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: forbes.com/profile/amancio-ortega/ names him, source of wealth 'Zara, Self Made', real-time rank #9 and net worth $149.5bn as fetched 2026-08-22 (the roster quoted #10 on the 2026 list; the live real-time page shows #9 -- same list, same person). Forbes's own one-line bio dates the business to 1975, which is the Zara store, not the venture; the manufacturing company is twelve years older. CURRENCY CONVERSION: 58.28 pesetas/US$, the 1973 average of the monthly FRED series EXSPUS (fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=EXSPUS). BOUNDED rev10 1963-1973, exactly at the frame's 10-year limit, both ends sourced. UPPER end: Luis Alonso Alvarez, 'Vistiendo a tres continentes: la ventaja competitiva del grupo Inditex-Zara, 1963-1999', Revista de Historia Industrial 18 (2000), p. 163: 'Se calcula que al cabo de diez anos, el grupo alcanzaba un volumen anual de ventas proximo a los 2.000 millones de pesetas' -- ten years after the 1963 founding of Confecciones GOA, i.e. 1973, group annual sales near 2,000 million pesetas = US$34.3M at 58.28, which is 2,488% of the 1973 nominal bar of $1,379,126 (rev10 = $10M constant 2026). Even at the pre-1971 official parity of 70 ptas/US$ it is $28.6M, 2,072% of the bar, so the conversion rate cannot change the verdict. LOWER end: the frame's founding-year rule -- Confecciones GOA was incorporated in 1963 and cannot have earned before it existed; the same paper describes it starting with its own factory of about 125 employees, growing to 380. QUALITATIVE-SCALE FLAG: the upper end is a single estimated figure ('se calcula', 'proximo a'), and the paper's own footnote 5 warns that 1963-1985 is hard to reconstruct because primary sources are scarce and the figures come largely from interviews with union officials and the group's chief executive. It is retained because the margin is roughly 25x -- the estimate would have to be wrong by a factor of twenty to move the verdict -- but the crossing year itself is genuinely unpinned inside the decade, hence the bound rather than a date. SERIAL FOUNDER CHECK: Confecciones GOA (1963) IS the first venture and IS the hit entity; Zara (first store 9 May 1975) and the Inditex holding (1985) are both later stages of the same business. Two earlier activities were checked and neither crosses: the informal family workshop making quilted housecoats at home before 1963, which no source dates or sizes and which the Historia Industrial paper describes only as the source of the savings for the 1963 jump; and the Sprint store opened on Calle Torreiro in 1971, which El Ideal Gallego records as a failure ('No funciona'). The 2001 IPO fallback is barred outright: an above-bar year is documented 28 years earlier. a2 FLAGGED: this is a DROPOUT YEAR, not a completed credential. Two sources (El Espanol, El Ideal Gallego) agree he left school at 14 to become an errand boy, which given his March 1936 birth is 1950; no source names any credential he completed, so this is recorded under the design spec's 'date of last formal credential, or of dropping out' at conf=low rather than left unknown. es.wikipedia says his textile career began at age 12, which would be 1948; the two Spanish press accounts saying 14 are preferred and the disagreement is why a3 is medium. a3: 1950, errand boy at the Gala shirt shop in A Coruna, three years there before moving to the La Maja haberdashery -- clothing retail, the same domain as the hit. a6: the May 2001 Inditex flotation.
